Oxera: Breath of fresh air in 2nd Covid wave

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
The second Covid wave has been far worse than the 1st and there are not enough hospital beds across the country never mind ICU beds or respirators. Afrox and Liquid Air barely have enough medical grade oxygen to keep up with demands having to increase their deliveries from once a week to daily supply consequently cutting back on supplying to their industrial customers. “ Oxera” Oxygen Efficient Respiratory Aid invented by an anesthetises at Frere Hospital has just been licenced by the SA Health Regulatory Authorities uses far less oxygen and has the potential to save lives.

Summary:
The standard treatment for COVID patients when admitted to hospital is to have oxygen administered through a basic cannular system, or even a mask but that’s very inefficient only getting 60% of the oxygen in, for extremely sick patients this is simply not a sufficient supply. Patients conditions are deteriorating quickly because of this and people are dying simply because there are not enough ICU beds or ventilators or adequately trained staff and people are dying unnecessarily simply because they can’t get oxygen efficiently into their collapsing lungs.
OXera is a simple device that administers high levels of oxygen through a mask, that is inflated and fits securely to the patients face. Using a bag and filter it pushes oxygen into the lungs preventing them from collapsing and making it easier for the intake of oxygen. The oxygen level can be regulated and increased according to the patients needs, it works quickly and does not require highly specialised staff. It can be used in a general wards and attached to the standard oxygen supply. Inspired by diving apparatus it had a valve which increases the pressure of oxygen to the lungs and a filter that prevents the virus being expelled into the air protecting medical staff and filters what the patient breaths in.


Further information:
Dr Craig Parker an anesthetist working at Frere hospital in East London in the COVID wards in the early days as the pandemic hit South Africa saw the desperate need for an intermediary device that was affordable and could be quickly administered to patients. With his background in Engineering, he started to work on a device that was cost effective and accessible to the 3rd world environment.
What’s critical with this device is that it is a far more efficient use of oxygen, it portable, and can use with a cylinder supply as well as main hospital supply of oxygen, so is extremely versatile. When the 2nd wave hit Europe he started to license the Oxera with SAHRA which finally came through at the end of December just in time as the 2nd wave started to peak in South Africa.
Parker has distributed them to rural hospitals like Zithulele and if he had his way be given away free across the country. 600 devices have been tested across and clinical trials being run in Gauteng while the registration
process unfolded. Gabler Medical have come on board and will start manufacturing 15 000 units a week. Its now a matter of getting Parker’s cost effective solution registered onto the Public Health supply chain which the NGO Right to Care has been working on and should be in place next

This is a single patient device and all that needs to be replaced is the filter which makes is extremely cost effective as medical equipment goes and doesn't require high levels of oxygen and air like ventilators which can only be used in an ICU environment. The beauty it it doesn't have expensive and complex mechanical parts

Provinces have discretionary funds and could easily acquire it and supply to clinics and not have to wait for the government tender processes


Extra Budget Items:
Cameraman return travel from PE R2400, only 1 flight a day in the middle of the day so I must fly in Sunday and get shooting while we wait for Derek to arrive so 3 nights accommodation for Producer. Pickup interview with Manufacturer in Cape Town which was part of Micheals shoot day so not sure if Derek will charge for that.

Script:


Script: The Eastern Cape is finally emerging from the 2nd Covid wave and medical staff are reeling, exhausted, and emotionally drained. Dr Raafiq Ely has been working in the Frere Hospital Covid ward in East London since last May, when the 1st Covid wave peaked. He says the 2nd wave, was far worse
Raafiq” We admitted about between 40 and 50 patients were tested covid positive over a 24 hour period. Sometimes our casualty area looked like a bomb exploded “
Script: It’s been no better in the private health sector, Dr Mike Webb was treating 200 patients between the 3 Life hospitals in East London
Webb: It's incredibly taxing emotionally, physically. Somebody called it a war zone today, that feeling of out of control.

Derek: You expect private care to be a level up, but not always know.

Webb: This pandemic has changed everything. I think the idea that just because you've got a medical aid, even money doesn't get you into an ICU.

Script: And for rural clinics like Madwaleni on the Wild Coast, at the end of a dirt road, the buck stops here. After 7 years, Dr John-D Lotz knows December is a tough time, when people return to their rural homes, and this December, was grim
John : We don't have the option of referring to an ICU or a high care setting either. So. That makes it really hard and hard on our patience, hard on our health care workers, especially the nurses here who spend the majority of time with our patients

Link: The situation at hospitals like Frere change virtually from day to day. At times beds and oxygen devices are available. But often life and death decisions have to be made with age and co-morbidities decreasing your chance of being at the front of the queue.
Raafiq “And I often caught myself thinking that I that I'm in this situation, we have to make death decisions instead of treatment decisions. And that part of dealing with Covid has been quite demoralizing.

Link: The 2nd wave has been so severe that it has caused an oxygen shortage around the country. Here at Frere Hospital they use an average of five tons a day...up to six last December. before Covid it was around a third of that amount before covid

Raafiq The problem is that that covid has some sort of pathological process that involves the lungs and it reduces the lungs ability to move oxygen to make it available to do the tissues for perfusion. So we give extra oxygen to overcome the pathology caused by covid.

Script: Afrox the major oxygen supplier to State hospitals is running out of oxygen across the country. They have diverted supplies from their industrial customers to meet the demand.
John : So for every patient on a facemask, you need three of those massive cylinders per day. And we in our ward during the peak and November, December, we had about 30, 35 patients in the ward. so if we use up all the oxygen covid patients, the rest of the hospital suffers as well
Link: Rural hospitals have been the hardest hit when it comes to oxygen . Some are dependent on cylinders being delivered by trucks at times stocks run so low they have to borrow from each other.
John : the depo at Umtata regularly struggles with transport issues, so they are only able to deliver it to us probably once every two weeks or so…., they can drop off about 40 or 60 cylinders of oxygen at a time. And it feels like Christmas when they do arrive. But failing that, we have to use hospital bakkies to trek to Umtata and back on a twice daily basis.
Script: Doctors are having to do the maths before making treatment decisions, if a critical patient needs 8 of the 20 oxygen cylinders on hand, with only a 1/3 chance of survival, who gets the oxygen? The pregnant women, the premature baby, or the 45 year old man?
John: So we start getting into the realm of ethics and distributive justice. Who do we justify giving that oxygen to?

Script: It’s exactly these nightmare decisions that Dr Craig Parker knows intimately, having done his community service at the oldest district hospital - Victoria, just outside Alice. But what’s unique about Dr Parker is he started out as a mechanical engineer, and became a doctor in his mid 40’s, now working in anaesthetics at Frere,East London Provincial Hospital
Craig So when it came to coronavirus and the pandemic unfolding around us, I felt that we we needed a unique South African solution to the problem. Something that used very little oxygen, needed to be affordable, and also needed to be able to be used by general nursing staff out there.

Script: In strict lockdown, a facebook post asking for some diving gear to experiment with, kicked it all off. A team of young techies, and designers with 3 d printers responded. Working over zoom and dropping off parts they had developed in each other's post boxes. Within 7 days they had the first design for OxERA - the Oxygen Efficient Respiratory Aid
Craig: I've been involved in most of the projects in South Africa around developing ventilator's in one form or another. and they are full of people with good intentions…. few of those have actually been able to deliver anything, anything meaningful.

Derek: Why is that?

Craig The doctors on the ground, we knew ventilators was not what we needed. It wasn't going to fix it. And so there's often a disconnect between engineering and medicine. And I guess having done both, it allows me to bridge them a little more naturally.

Script: Oxera has filled a gap between basic oxygen therapy, with an oxygen mask, and high end care, like Ventilators. It's simple design belies it’s genius. An inflatable rim fits tightly around the face, stopping valuable oxygen from escaping, which happens with normal masks. A pressure value, keeps the lungs from collapsing, and a filter stops virus transmission. Using 15 litres a minute working off cylinders or piped oxygen.
The reason it is a game changer, is that it extends the range of therapy available at a basic facility, preventing the need for high end oxygen therapy which uses 60 litres a minute.

John “We just realized how amazing they are for two reasons. The first was that they use as much oxygen as a facemask. I didn't need to make an ethical decision to change onto Oxera mask I could just provide it. And the second reason is that it seemed to perform about as well as our CPap devices or our high flow nasal prong and suddenly we realized that we could and fulfill both needs, we could step up our of care for people without it costing oxygen for other patients. And filling that gap is amazing.

Raafiq. I had a patient come to my ward, an elderly gentleman, multiple comorbidities, obese they were wheeling into the ward and I said, oh my God, but this guy is busy dying. His oxygen saturation is about 20 percent and I applied the device and within half an hour his saturation improved to 97 percent. I mean, eight days later, the same patient I thought was dying in front of my eyes was actually discharged from hospital.

Script; All the doctors are clear these are only anecdotal observations. Clinical trials began at Baragwanath hospital as soon as the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority licenced it, in late December. But for doctors on the frontline faced with insufficient ICU beds and nursing staff it’s been a lifesaver. Mike Webb immediately went out and got 20 devices for his private patients.
Webb: It buys you time in those patients that need support to get them through 24, forty eight, seventy two hours until an ICU bed opens and you can get them in
Script: “Vanessa Fisher is Dr Webb’s patient admitted just after Christmas to Life Beacon Bay, her oxygen saturation levels were critically low, and the longer she remained like that, the more tissue damage

Webb ”I remember saying to her that if we don't make a plan to get her oxygen levels up, she was going to be in very deep trouble and quite possibly die.

Derek: Vanessa, what was it like wearing that mask.

Vanessa “You almost have an anxiety attack because it just can't do anything but have this thing on your face. I kept telling myself, it's your job to breathe, thats all you have to do

Derek: Do you think this device actually helped save your life?

Vanessa: 100% If it hadn't been for that Oxera mask, I don't think that I don't think that I'd be here speaking to you now.

Script: Craig’s established a social enterprise - Umoyo, ploughing any profits into subsidising or sponsoring the device. Donating over 600 masks to rural and tertiary hospitals, turning this home into an assembly line while waiting for the registration. As fast as they could put them together, they were flying out the door.
Initially Craig wanted everyone to be able to print their own Oxera, but realising his open-source design needed support, they partnered with Reiner Gabler of Gabler Medical who produce 15 000 a week.
Reiner “ it's a positive message for local manufacture of medical devices in this country, because I think it's been pretty obvious during the Covid crisis that we actually have a shortage of uh, local manufacturers. Success stories like this one should encourage other designers and other developers to enter the medical device field
Derek: Doctor, if you could speak to the health minister right now, would you try to speed up the process of getting Oxera delivered around the country?
Raafiq I would literally beg to see Oxera available, I would take this device and carry it in my bag as an emergency device
Craig: A lot of pressure from the ground up saying, please, we need these as soon as we can, please hurry up that process so we're working as best we can with government to get that loop closed so that these can be put in the hands of the patients who need them.
Script: Considering that half of South Africa population is rural, and the vaccine is a way off, Craig and his team have given health care workers another arrow in their quiver, in a resource constrained county
Craig “You know, when we get those reports back that your device saved another life, it's phenomenal.

Promo: Covid patients are dying because of lack of ICU beds and oxygen supplies in rural hospitals. An invention by an Eastern Cape doctor is bringing hope to both patients and doctors alike.
Promo: A low tech oxygen mask invented by an Eastern Cape doctor is saving lives. Designed for the general ward with minimal oxygen, it’s doing the job of expensive high tech alternatives.
Promo: A simple oxygen mask designed by an Eastern Cape doctor is changing how medical staff are treating their seriously ill Covid patients. Its saving lives and critical oxygen supplies

metadata.Unique Selling Point: The second Covid wave has been far worse than the 1st and there are not enough hospital beds across the country never mind ICU beds or respirators. Afrox and Liquid Air barely have enough medical grade oxygen to keep up with demands having to increase their deliveries from once a week to daily supply consequently cutting back on supplying to their industrial customers. “ Oxera” Oxygen Efficient Respiratory Aid invented by an anesthetises at Frere Hospital has just been licenced by the SA Health Regulatory Authorities uses far less oxygen and has the potential to save lives.
metadata.Summary: The standard treatment for COVID patients when admitted to hospital is to have oxygen administered through a basic cannular system, or even a mask but that’s very inefficient only getting 60% of the oxygen in, for extremely sick patients this is simply not a sufficient supply. Patients conditions are deteriorating quickly because of this and people are dying simply because there are not enough ICU beds or ventilators or adequately trained staff and people are dying unnecessarily simply because they can’t get oxygen efficiently into their collapsing lungs. OXera is a simple device that administers high levels of oxygen through a mask, that is inflated and fits securely to the patients face. Using a bag and filter it pushes oxygen into the lungs preventing them from collapsing and making it easier for the intake of oxygen. The oxygen level can be regulated and increased according to the patients needs, it works quickly and does not require highly specialised staff. It can be used in a general wards and attached to the standard oxygen supply. Inspired by diving apparatus it had a valve which increases the pressure of oxygen to the lungs and a filter that prevents the virus being expelled into the air protecting medical staff and filters what the patient breaths in.
metadata.Further information: Dr Craig Parker an anesthetist working at Frere hospital in East London in the COVID wards in the early days as the pandemic hit South Africa saw the desperate need for an intermediary device that was affordable and could be quickly administered to patients. With his background in Engineering, he started to work on a device that was cost effective and accessible to the 3rd world environment. What’s critical with this device is that it is a far more efficient use of oxygen, it portable, and can use with a cylinder supply as well as main hospital supply of oxygen, so is extremely versatile. When the 2nd wave hit Europe he started to license the Oxera with SAHRA which finally came through at the end of December just in time as the 2nd wave started to peak in South Africa. Parker has distributed them to rural hospitals like Zithulele and if he had his way be given away free across the country. 600 devices have been tested across and clinical trials being run in Gauteng while the registration process unfolded. Gabler Medical have come on board and will start manufacturing 15 000 units a week. Its now a matter of getting Parker’s cost effective solution registered onto the Public Health supply chain which the NGO Right to Care has been working on and should be in place next This is a single patient device and all that needs to be replaced is the filter which makes is extremely cost effective as medical equipment goes and doesn't require high levels of oxygen and air like ventilators which can only be used in an ICU environment. The beauty it it doesn't have expensive and complex mechanical parts Provinces have discretionary funds and could easily acquire it and supply to clinics and not have to wait for the government tender processes
